opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that collective action problems aren't laws of physics. People talk about them as if they're inevitable, as if the race dynamic is just baked into reality and there's nothing anyone can do. But humanity has solved collective action problems before. We did it with nuclear weapons, imperfectly, but we did it. We did it with CFCs and the ozone layer. We did it with biological weapons, human cloning, and a whole bunch of other things where in principle there was an incentive for someone to defect, and yet we built institutions, norms, and treaties that made defection costly and cooperation the default.

So the question isn't whether it's possible. The question is whether we're willing to do the boring, unglamorous work of actually building those institutions. And I think the main obstacle right now isn't some deep game-theoretic impossibility. It's that the people with the most influence, the people building these systems, have a very strong incentive to tell everyone the problem is unsolvable. "If we don't build it, China will." "If we don't race, someone worse will." That's a very convenient story if you're the one racing.

What actually gets you out of a collective action problem is common knowledge. Everyone needs to know that everyone else knows the danger, and that there are credible mechanisms to verify that others aren't defecting. With AI you have real chokepoints. Frontier development requires enormous amounts of compute, very specialized chips, a tiny number of fabs, and a handful of companies. That's far more tractable than people pretend. You can monitor compute, require licensing above certain thresholds, and build international agreements around that.

And frankly, a lot of this starts domestically. You don't need a perfect global treaty on day one. You need countries, starting with the ones where the frontier labs actually are, to say: "We are not going to allow private companies to build systems that could be catastrophically dangerous without oversight." Once a few major players do that, it becomes much easier to bring others along, because you've changed the default.

The other piece is citizens. Politicians respond to what people care about, and right now most people don't know that the explicit goal of these companies is to build systems smarter than all humans, and that the people building them openly say there's a meaningful chance this goes catastrophically wrong. When people learn that, they're usually horrified, and rightly so. So a huge part of escaping the trap is just telling people the truth and letting democratic processes do what they're supposed to do.

It's not hopeless. It's hard, but hard is different from hopeless. The worst thing we can do is accept the fatalistic framing, because that framing is itself what keeps the trap closed.

r001.rationale: The response says countries can act domestically before a global treaty exists, and that action by a few major players can change the default and help bring others along.

r002.rationale: It does not propose country contingency plans triggered by clear evidence that another country is allowing existentially risky technology to be built.

r003.rationale: It discusses compute monitoring and licensing, but does not propose a government-controlled mechanism to shut down AI compute clusters.

r004.rationale: The response does not call for periodically testing emergency shutdowns of compute clusters.

r005.rationale: It does not propose making an international AI treaty take effect after participation reaches specified thresholds.

r006.rationale: It does not identify coalition members' share of world GDP as a source of competitive leverage.

r007.rationale: It does not identify coalition members' share of world population as a basis for treaty legitimacy.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the collective action framing is correct, and most people who use it then immediately draw the wrong conclusion from it. They say, "Well, it's a coordination problem, so it's hopeless, so we might as well race." And that's just not how humans have handled coordination problems historically. We've banned chemical weapons. We've banned human cloning, basically globally, with almost no enforcement apparatus. We did the Montreal Protocol on CFCs. None of these were magic. They happened because a relatively small number of people decided that the thing was unacceptable, made that legible to the public and to governments, and then the equilibrium shifted.

The thing that makes a collective action problem tractable is that everyone involved actually believes the outcome of not coordinating is bad for them personally. Right now, the people racing don't believe that, or more precisely, they've convinced themselves that they're the responsible ones and so the race is fine as long as they win it. Every lab tells the same story: "We don't like this, but if we don't do it, someone worse will." And you hear that from all of them simultaneously. That's not a stable argument, that's a confession. It's a group of people telling you they're trapped in a bad equilibrium and asking you to please not intervene.

So the way you escape it is not that you ask the labs nicely. You don't solve prisoner's dilemmas by asking the prisoners to be more virtuous. You change the payoff structure from the outside. That means governments, that means law, that means actual enforcement with teeth. And here I think people massively underestimate how much leverage exists. Frontier AI is one of the most concentrated, legible, physically bottlenecked industries on the planet. There are a handful of companies, a handful of chip fabs, a handful of data centers that you can literally see from space, and an enormous amount of capital that needs legal protection to exist. This is not like trying to regulate a thousand people with laptops. This is closer to regulating nuclear enrichment than regulating software.

The second thing I'd say is that the collective action problem is partly manufactured. The "China will do it anyway" argument gets deployed as if it were an immutable fact of nature, and when you actually talk to people who work on China policy, the picture is far more mixed. The Chinese government does not love uncontrollable technologies that could destabilize the Party. There's genuine common interest there, and nobody has seriously tried to build on it, partly because it's convenient for the labs if everyone assumes negotiation is impossible.

And then the third piece, which I think is the one people find least satisfying, is that the actual bottleneck is narrative. Right now the public conversation is dominated by people who have a direct financial stake in the race continuing, and they've been very effective at making the whole thing sound either inevitable or like science fiction. If normal people, and normal politicians, understood what the people building these systems privately say about them, the collective action problem would look very different, because the political cost of doing nothing would go way up. Governments move when their constituents are afraid and when inaction is visibly blamed on them. That's not cynical, that's just how democratic incentives work, and it's the lever that actually exists.

So, short version: you don't escape the collective action problem by hoping for cooperation to emerge spontaneously among the racers. You escape it by making the race illegal, making that enforceable, and making it politically costly to be the person who didn't do that. That's hard. It's not impossible. We've done harder things with far less at stake.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to stop treating this as a problem that individual good intentions can solve. You can have people inside every lab who sincerely care about safety, and still get a race where everyone feels compelled to do something dangerous because they expect someone else to do it first. That’s a problem with the incentives.

So you need agreements that are verifiable and enforceable. It’s not enough for companies to say, “We’ll be responsible.” You need them to be able to say, “We’ll accept these restrictions, provided our competitors are subject to them too, and there’s a credible way to check.” That’s one of the things government is supposed to make possible.

Internationally, that’s obviously harder. But a collective action problem isn’t a proof that cooperation is impossible. The question is whether the participants recognize a shared interest in avoiding an outcome that none of them can control. If you frame this exclusively as a contest to win, you obscure that shared interest. Being first to build something you can’t control isn’t much of a victory.

I’d start with transparency around the largest training runs, independent oversight, and the actual authority to stop a project when the evidence warrants it. Then build international agreements around restrictions that can be monitored. None of that guarantees success. But it starts changing the incentives, rather than asking everybody to be extraordinarily virtuous while rewarding them for racing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to make cooperation enforceable. If every company says, “Well, we’d love to slow down, but the other companies won’t,” and every country says the same thing about other countries, you’ve created a system where everyone feels compelled to do something they think might be disastrous. Asking the individual actors to be more virtuous doesn’t resolve that incentive structure.

That’s one of the reasons we have governments and international agreements. You need rules that apply to everybody, ways to verify that people are following them, and consequences for breaking them. For advanced AI, compute is a potentially useful place to do that, because the largest training runs depend on physical infrastructure. It gives you something more concrete to monitor than a promise to be responsible.

Of course, then you ask: why would governments agree? Well, the important possibility is that they have a shared interest in avoiding systems they can’t control. You don’t need everyone to agree on politics or values to agree that losing control would be bad for them.

That doesn’t make an agreement easy. Verification is hard, trust is limited, and there are real competitive pressures. But those are the problems governance has to solve. You have to build a situation where exercising restraint doesn’t mean unilaterally surrendering an advantage, because the other actors are bound by the same constraints.

r001.rationale: It argues for enforceable mutual constraints so restraint does not mean unilateral surrender; it does not propose restructuring the problem to enable unilateral action.
